data-classification.overview: Data classification is the step that decides what protection something deserves. Without it, every item is treated the same way, which usually means the sensitive items are not protected enough.
how_it_works: Classification assigns a level based on sensitivity and the harm disclosure would cause.
Each level maps to controls: where the data may be stored, who may see it, how it is encrypted, and how long it is kept.
Classification is only useful if the mapping to controls is written down and enforced by systems.
The hardest part is usually deciding the level for new data, and getting people to label it consistently.
Retention is part of classification, because data nobody needs should not exist at all.
history: Physical filing systems used clear markings like confidential, which translated directly once data became digital.
Regulatory definitions introduced formal categories tied to specific legal obligations rather than to intuition.
Cloud storage made it technically easy to apply different controls per classification, which turned policy into configuration.
Data discovery tooling emerged because nobody actually knew where all the sensitive data lived.
real_world: A spreadsheet of customer records in a general-purpose shared folder is the most common classification failure in practice.
Data that is correctly classified but stored without encryption loses its protection the moment storage is misconfigured.
Labeling that depends on the user's judgement produces wildly inconsistent results across a large organisation.
what_to_look_for: Check whether a written classification scheme exists and whether the levels map to specific controls.
Check where the most sensitive data actually lives, rather than where policy says it should.
Check whether retention periods are defined and enforced, rather than being indefinite by default.
Check whether classification is applied automatically where it can be, rather than relying on users to label files.
defensive: Define a small number of levels and map each one to concrete technical controls.
Discover where sensitive data actually is, because you cannot protect data you have not found.
Apply classification automatically by pattern or by location, and let users only correct it.
Set retention periods and enforce deletion, because unretained data cannot leak.
Re-classify when data is aggregated, since combining two ordinary records can create a sensitive one.

encryption-at-rest-transit-and-backup.overview: Encryption helps in three separate places, and each covers a different failure. Encrypting only in transit leaves the most common leak paths completely unprotected.
how_it_works: In transit protects data while it moves between systems, and this is what HTTPS provides.
At rest protects stored data, so a stolen disk or a compromised storage account does not yield plaintext.
Backups need protection too, because a backup is a full copy of everything you were trying to protect.
Encryption only helps if the key is protected separately from the data, or the two are compromised together.
Full-disk and application-level encryption solve different problems, since one protects a device and the other a specific field.
history: Encryption at rest was expensive and so was applied to databases and backups rather than to laptops.
Storage vendors began offering encryption by default, which removed the cost barrier and the decision.
Cloud platforms added server-side encryption options, often on by default but not always for every service.
Asynchronous replication made it necessary to encrypt backups separately, since a snapshot is a new copy of the data.
real_world: A lost laptop with an unencrypted disk turns into a data breach report, regardless of how good the rest of the system is.
A database with encrypted columns but backups in the clear means the breach simply happens at restore time.
A customer-managed key stored in the same account as the data it protects provides almost no benefit.
what_to_look_for: Check whether encryption is enabled on every store that holds sensitive data, including backups and logs.
Check where the keys live and who can read them.
Check whether backups are encrypted separately from the source system.
Check device-level encryption, since portable devices are the ones that get lost.
defensive: Encrypt everything that holds sensitive data, including backups, replicas and exported extracts.
Keep keys separate from the data, and control key access more tightly than data access.
Enable full-disk encryption on every portable device and require it by policy.
Encrypt data in transit on every connection, including internal ones and backups sent off site.
Verify that a backup is encrypted by restoring from it, rather than by reading the configuration.

malware-families.overview: Malware names describe how something spreads and what it does. Knowing the families is useful mainly because each one implies a different set of controls that would have stopped it.
how_it_works: A virus attaches itself to a file and needs the file to be run, which is why it faded as executable-only systems became rare.
A worm spreads by itself across a network, so containment matters more than detection per machine.
A trojan poses as something legitimate and relies on the user running it, so user-facing controls matter most.
Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment, and its modern form also steals the data first.
Fileless and living-off-the-land techniques run through tools already installed, which is why file-based detection misses them.
history: Early malware relied on floppy disks and shared filesystems, which is why the virus category dominated for decades.
Email and macro-enabled documents created a huge wave of trojans as email replaced physical media.
Polymorphic engines defeated signature detection, and packers were used to hide the real content of a file.
Fileless execution and living-off-the-land techniques shifted the problem toward behavioural detection.
real_world: A worm inside a flat network can reach most systems before anyone notices, which is why segmentation is the main control.
A trojan delivered as an invoice attachment succeeds because the context makes it look expected.
Ransomware that also exfiltrates data gives the attacker leverage even if you restore cleanly.
what_to_look_for: Check that segmentation would actually contain a worm or a ransomware spread.
Check how email attachments and macros are handled, since that is the most common initial delivery.
Check whether behavioural detection is enabled, since file scanning alone misses modern techniques.
Check how quickly you could isolate a machine, because response speed limits most outbreaks.
defensive: Segment the network so a single infected machine cannot reach everything.
Block macros by default and treat attachments from outside the organisation as untrusted.
Use behavioural detection and application control rather than relying on file signatures.
Keep offline or immutable backups, so encryption of the live systems cannot reach the copies.
Practice isolating a machine, because an unproven containment plan does not contain anything.

malware-delivery-and-initial-access.overview: Initial access is the step defenders most often miss. If you know how things are getting in, you can remove the route instead of chasing every payload.
how_it_works: Delivery is the mechanism: an attachment, a link, a compromised website, or a malicious update.
The payload then executes with the privileges of whoever opened it, which is usually a person.
Living in memory rather than on disk shortens the window in which a file scan can see anything.
A remote access tool installed afterwards gives persistent hands-on control while looking like a normal tool.
Most intrusions leave a visible trace at delivery, and that trace is the most reliable detection point available.
history: Physical media and unpatched services were the usual routes before widespread internet access.
Email became the dominant delivery channel, and remains so despite years of predictions to the contrary.
Compromised legitimate websites made delivery look like ordinary browsing.
Supply-chain compromise shifted delivery upstream, so the update mechanism itself became the vector.
real_world: A fake invoice with an attachment is still one of the most common first steps in a real intrusion.
An unpatched internet-facing service is often the route, and it is discoverable within hours of appearing.
A third-party update mechanism with broad permissions can distribute malicious code to every customer at once.
what_to_look_for: Check which external services are reachable and what they expose.
Check how email attachments and links are handled, and whether reporting is easy.
Check for software with update rights far beyond what it needs.
Check whether a remote access tool is installed anywhere it should not be.
defensive: Reduce reachable surface first, since an unreachable service cannot be the entry point.
Handle email attachments deliberately: block by default, or require a reason to open.
Give update mechanisms only the permission they need, and monitor what they change.
Alert on remote access software being installed, since that is rarely legitimate.
Make reporting something easy, because speed matters more than perfect filtering.

ransomware-double-extortion-and-recovery.overview: Modern ransomware usually does two things: it encrypts the data and it copies it first. The copy is what creates pressure, because the victim can restore but cannot be sure the data was not taken.
how_it_works: Initial access is followed by a period of quiet activity while the attacker prepares, which is the most useful detection window.
Data is often exfiltrated before encryption, so the theft is complete even if every system is restored.
Encryption then disrupts operations, usually in batches so recovery is deliberately painful.
Backups that share credentials or network access with production are often reached by the same attacker.
Recovery is a business decision under pressure, which is exactly when paying becomes tempting.
history: Early ransomware encrypted one machine at a time and was largely a nuisance.
Crypto-ransomware made payment meaningful, and criminal groups built around it.
Exfiltration before encryption introduced the double-extortion model and changed the negotiation position.
Ransomware-as-a-service lowered the skill barrier, and affiliate models scaled it.
real_world: An organisation that restores quickly still has to act on the assumption that data was taken.
Backups reachable with the same domain administrator account as production are effectively inside the blast radius.
A network share used for file access can be encrypted far faster than a server, and it is where business data usually lives.
what_to_look_for: Check whether backups are isolated from production in both credentials and network path.
Check whether the backup catalogue itself is protected, since deleting backups defeats everything.
Check how long a full restore would actually take, measured rather than assumed.
Check whether the decision-making path for a ransomware incident is written down and known.
defensive: Keep backups immutable or offline, so encryption cannot reach them.
Use separate credentials for backup administration, so one compromise does not do both.
Test full restores on a schedule and record the real elapsed time.
Segment aggressively, because most ransomware is stopped by containment rather than recovery.
Decide the response criteria in advance, when nobody is panicking, and rehearse it.

backups-3-2-1-and-tested-restores.overview: A backup that has never been restored is a hypothesis, not a control. The rule of three copies is well known; the part everyone gets wrong is the test.
how_it_works: Three copies means the original plus two backups, so one failure is survivable.
Two media means the copies are not all on the same device that can fail together.
One off site means a fire, theft or ransomware at the primary location does not destroy everything.
Incremental and full backups trade speed against restore time, since a restore of many incrementals is slower.
Retention determines what point you can return to, so a ransomware event may exceed the shortest retention.
history: Backups were tape-based, offsite by definition, and slow enough that testing was routine.
Cheap disk arrays made local backups affordable and, with them, the assumption that the copy was safe.
Synchronised storage made replication continuous, which quietly turned a backup into a mirror of the primary.
Ransomware made immutability the main requirement, because anything writable by the attacker is not a backup.
real_world: A synchronised folder is not a backup, since deletion or encryption propagates to the copy immediately.
A restore that has never been timed turns a four-hour outage into a four-day outage.
Backups with a retention shorter than the attacker's dwell time can be entirely deleted before anyone notices.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the backup copy is genuinely separate, or synchronised to the primary.
Check whether backups are protected from deletion by the same credentials that run production.
Check the last time a full restore was actually performed and timed.
Check the retention period against the time an attacker could plausibly remain undetected.
defensive: Follow three copies, two media, one off site, and make the off-site copy immutable.
Use separate credentials for backup administration and require multi-factor authentication on it.
Test restores regularly and record the real elapsed time for a full recovery.
Alert on backup deletion, since that is a strong indicator of an ongoing incident.
Include configuration and identity data in backups, since restoring only data often leaves a system unusable.

personal-data-and-minimisation.overview: Data protection law is built on a simple idea: collect and keep only what you actually need. Everything else is liability you chose to take on.
how_it_works: Personal data is any information relating to an identified or identifiable person, which is broader than people assume.
Collecting less reduces the impact of a breach, because there is less to disclose.
Retention limits exposure in time as well as in size, since old data is still a liability.
Sharing with a processor transfers responsibility, which is why contracts and instructions matter.
Individual rights such as access and deletion require the ability to find and remove a person data across systems.
history: Early privacy regulation was sector-specific and focused on records held by organisations.
Broader modern regulation treats data protection as a default across all processing.
Data minimisation moved from a recommendation to an obligation in several jurisdictions.
The practical difficulty of honouring individual rights across many systems is what drives current tooling.
real_world: A marketing database that was never needed becomes the largest disclosure in a breach.
Data retained for a made-up future purpose cannot be justified when a request arrives.
A processor breach becomes your breach from the regulator's point of view if you did not control the contract.
what_to_look_for: Check what personal data is actually held, and whether each purpose is still real.
Check the retention schedule and whether anything is kept indefinitely by default.
Check which processors hold data and under what written instructions.
Check whether you could find and delete a specific person data on request.
defensive: Collect only what a stated purpose requires, and write that purpose down.
Set retention periods and automate deletion rather than reviewing manually.
Keep a record of processing so you can answer questions about any dataset.
Use written contracts with processors and verify they are followed.
Build the ability to find and delete a person's data across all systems that hold it.

device-security-locking-wiping-and-mobil.overview: Devices leave the building, and that is the whole problem. Encryption, screen locks and remote wipe only work together, because each addresses a different loss scenario.
how_it_works: Full-disk encryption means a lost device does not leak its contents if it is powered off.
A screen lock and a strong unlock credential are what make that encryption effective in practice.
A PIN or pattern is far weaker than a passphrase, and a short one is brute-forceable quickly.
Remote wipe requires the device to be online and enrolled, so it fails when the device is off or unconnected.
Mobile platforms apply their own protections, but managed-device settings change what an organisation can enforce.
history: Devices were rarely encrypted, and a lost laptop was treated as a lost laptop rather than a data event.
Full-disk encryption became standard on laptops as hardware support matured.
Mobile platforms introduced hardware-backed key storage and strong defaults by default.
Mobile device management added the ability to enforce settings, which only works if the device is enrolled.
real_world: An encrypted laptop with no screen lock is barely better than an unencrypted one, because the key is already in memory.
A four-digit code can be tried quickly enough that a short PIN is effectively no protection.
A device that is out of remote-wipe range cannot be wiped, which is why the recovery plan needs a second step.
what_to_look_for: Check whether full-disk encryption is enabled on every portable device.
Check the screen-lock timeout and whether the unlock credential is a passphrase rather than a short PIN.
Check which devices are enrolled for remote management and which are not.
Check what happens if remote wipe fails, since a second procedure is required.
defensive: Require full-disk encryption and a strong screen lock on every portable device.
Prefer a passphrase over a PIN, and require multi-factor authentication where the platform supports it.
Enrol every device in remote management, and verify the wipe path has been tested.
Keep short automatic lock timeouts, since an unattended device is an unlocked device.
Revoke certificates and sessions on the device when it is lost, so a wipe is not the only defence.

secure-disposal-and-sanitisation.overview: Data that is deleted but still recoverable is not deleted. Disposal has to match the medium and the sensitivity of what was on it.
how_it_works: Deleting a file removes the reference, not the content, and the data usually remains on the medium.
Overwriting can work on a traditional drive but is unreliable on flash and on wear-levelled storage.
Full-disk encryption changes the problem: once the key is destroyed, the data is unrecoverable regardless of the medium.
Physical destruction is the only certain method, and it matters most for small volumes of highly sensitive data.
Retention matters most of all, because a drive that never held the data cannot leak it.
history: Overwriting was the standard method when magnetic drives were the norm and traces were readable.
Flash storage introduced remapping layers that defeat overwriting entirely.
Full-disk encryption shifted the focus to key destruction, which is cheaper and verifiable.
Cloud services made disposal a contractual and logical question rather than a physical one.
real_world: A formatted drive that was encrypted and then had its key destroyed is safe, while a formatted unencrypted drive is not.
Discarded phones and drives are a routine source of data exposure because the wipe was never performed.
A backup provider retaining data past the contract end is a common and easily missed exposure.
what_to_look_for: Check how devices are disposed of, and whether the process is documented and witnessed.
Check whether drives were encrypted, since that changes the correct disposal method.
Check whether backups and cloud copies are included in the disposal process, not just the primary device.
Check for media in recycling and storage that was never processed at all.
defensive: Encrypt every drive that holds sensitive data, so disposal reduces to destroying keys.
Use a documented and witnessed process for any medium that cannot be encrypted.
Cryptographically erase where the platform supports it, and record the certificate that proves it.
Include backups, cloud copies and returned equipment in the disposal process.
Prefer retaining less, because disposal is only necessary for what was kept.
